subject: biology
overview: Unit 6 covers sexual reproduction in flowering plants, human reproduction and reproductive health. It runs from flower structure, gametophytes, pollination, double fertilization and seed formation to human gametogenesis, the menstrual cycle, pregnancy, contraception, STIs and assisted reproductive technologies. NEET asks about 8-10 questions from this unit every year, almost all line-based from NCERT, so precise facts, examples and sequences score directly.

topics.explanation: The flower is the site of sexual reproduction in angiosperms. The androecium is the whorl of stamens, and each stamen has a filament and an anther. A typical anther is bilobed and dithecous, meaning each lobe has two thecae. In transverse section it is tetragonal with four microsporangia, one at each corner, which develop into pollen sacs. The gynoecium is the female whorl. It may be monocarpellary or multicarpellary, and multicarpellary gynoecia are either syncarpous (fused carpels, as in Papaver) or apocarpous (free carpels, as in Michelia). Each pistil has a stigma (landing platform for pollen), a style and a basal swollen ovary. The ovarian cavity (locule) holds ovules attached to the placenta. The number of ovules ranges from one (wheat, paddy, mango) to many (papaya, watermelon, orchids).
key_points: Anther is bilobed and dithecous, with 4 microsporangia (tetrasporangiate)
Filament is attached to the thalamus or to a petal
Pistil consists of stigma, style and ovary
Syncarpous gynoecium: Papaver; apocarpous gynoecium: Michelia
Single ovule: wheat, paddy, mango; many ovules: papaya, watermelon, orchids

formulas.meaning: Counting thecae or microsporangia in a typical anther

topics.neet_tip: NEET asks counting questions (thecae per lobe = 2, microsporangia per anther = 4) and examples of single or multi-ovuled ovaries.

topics.explanation: Microsporogenesis: the wall of a microsporangium has four layers, from outside inward the epidermis, endothecium, middle layers and tapetum. The outer three layers protect the sporangium and help dehiscence. The tapetum nourishes the developing pollen; its cells have dense cytoplasm and often more than one nucleus. Sporogenous tissue forms microspore mother cells, which undergo meiosis to give microspore tetrads, which mature into pollen grains. The exine is made of sporopollenin, the most resistant organic material known, and has germ pores where sporopollenin is absent. The intine is made of cellulose and pectin. A mature pollen grain has a large vegetative cell and a small generative cell; the generative cell later divides to form two male gametes. Megasporogenesis: inside the ovule, a megaspore mother cell in the micropylar region of the nucellus divides by meiosis to give four megaspores. Three degenerate, so development is monosporic. The surviving functional megaspore undergoes three free-nuclear mitoses, giving an 8-nucleate, 7-celled embryo sac.
key_points: Microsporangium wall from outside: epidermis, endothecium, middle layers, tapetum (innermost, nutritive)
Exine is sporopollenin, which resists high temperature, strong acids, alkalis and enzymes
Over 60% of angiosperms shed pollen at the 2-celled stage; the rest shed it at the 3-celled stage
Pollen viability is about 30 minutes in rice and wheat but months in Rosaceae, Leguminosae and Solanaceae
Pollen can be stored in liquid nitrogen at $-196^\circ C$ in pollen banks
Ovule parts: funicle, hilum, integuments, micropyle, chalaza, nucellus, embryo sac
Embryo sac: egg apparatus (2 synergids plus 1 egg) at the micropylar end, 3 antipodals at the chalazal end, and a central cell with 2 polar nuclei
Synergids carry the filiform apparatus, which guides the pollen tube
Pollen of Parthenium (carrot grass) causes allergy

formulas.meaning: One microspore mother cell gives 4 pollen grains
One megaspore mother cell gives only 1 functional megaspore, so 1 meiosis per embryo sac
Free-nuclear divisions of the functional megaspore

topics.neet_tip: Expect questions on the role of the synergids and filiform apparatus, the composition of exine, the tapetum, and the 8-nucleate 7-celled embryo sac.
topics.topic: Development of male and female gametophytes

topics.explanation: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains to the stigma. There are three types. Autogamy uses pollen from the same flower. Geitonogamy uses pollen from another flower of the same plant; it is functionally cross-pollination but genetically similar to autogamy. Xenogamy uses pollen from a different plant and is the only type that brings genetically different pollen. Chasmogamous flowers have exposed anthers and stigma. Cleistogamous flowers never open, so they are invariably autogamous and assure seed set; examples are Viola, Oxalis and Commelina. Abiotic agents are wind and water. Biotic agents are animals, mainly insects (especially bees), as well as birds, bats, rodents and lizards. Wind-pollinated flowers produce light, non-sticky pollen, have well-exposed stamens, large feathery stigmas and often a single ovule; examples are grasses and maize. Water pollination occurs in about 30 genera, mostly monocots.
key_points: Wind pollination: grasses, maize (tassels are the stigma and style)
Water pollination: Vallisneria, Hydrilla, Zostera (marine seagrass)
In Vallisneria, pollen is released on the water surface and the long-stalked female flowers reach the surface
In seagrasses, the long ribbon-like pollen grains are carried inside the water
Water hyacinth and water lily are aquatic but are pollinated by insects or wind
Insect-pollinated flowers are large, colourful, fragrant and nectar-rich
Amorphophallus has a flower about 6 feet tall
Yucca and a moth species are mutually dependent; the moth lays eggs in the locule
Floral rewards are nectar and pollen; bees are the dominant biotic pollinators
Some insects, called pollen or nectar robbers, take rewards without pollinating
topics.neet_tip: Match-the-column questions on agent versus example (Vallisneria, Zostera, maize, Yucca, Amorphophallus) and on cleistogamy are very frequent.

topics.explanation: Continuous self-pollination causes inbreeding depression, so plants have outbreeding devices. In some species pollen release and stigma receptivity are not synchronised. In others the anther and stigma are placed at different positions. Self-incompatibility is a genetic mechanism that prevents self-pollen (from the same flower or other flowers of the same plant) from fertilising the ovules, by inhibiting pollen germination or pollen tube growth in the pistil. Unisexual flowers also help. In monoecious plants such as castor and maize, autogamy is prevented but geitonogamy is not. In dioecious plants such as papaya, both autogamy and geitonogamy are prevented. Pollen-pistil interaction is the dynamic process by which the pistil recognises compatible pollen through chemical components of the pollen and the pistil. Compatible pollen germinates, and the pollen tube grows through a germ pore, down the stigma and style, and enters the ovule through the micropyle. It then enters one synergid through the filiform apparatus. Plant breeders use artificial hybridization, which involves emasculation (removing anthers from bisexual flowers before dehiscence) followed by bagging.
key_points: Outbreeding devices: non-synchrony of pollen release and stigma receptivity, different positioning, self-incompatibility, unisexuality
Monoecious plants (castor, maize) prevent autogamy only
Dioecious plants (papaya) prevent both autogamy and geitonogamy
Pollen tube enters a synergid via the filiform apparatus
Emasculation is needed only for bisexual flowers; unisexual female flowers are only bagged
Rebagging is done after dusting pollen on the stigma
topics.neet_tip: NEET often asks which plant prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy (papaya) and the steps of an artificial hybridization programme.

topics.explanation: The pollen tube releases two male gametes into the cytoplasm of a synergid. One male gamete fuses with the egg cell; this is syngamy and forms a diploid zygote. The other male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei in the central cell; this is triple fusion and forms a triploid primary endosperm nucleus (PEN). The central cell then becomes the primary endosperm cell. Because two fusions occur in one embryo sac, the process is called double fertilization, and it is unique to angiosperms. The zygote develops into the embryo and the PEN develops into the endosperm.
key_points: Syngamy: male gamete plus egg gives the zygote ($2n$)
Triple fusion: male gamete plus 2 polar nuclei gives the PEN ($3n$)
Double fertilization is a characteristic feature of angiosperms
Each ovule needs one pollen grain, which carries 2 male gametes

formulas.meaning: If $2n = 36$, then $n = 18$ and the endosperm has $3n = 54$ chromosomes
Each fertilized ovule uses two male gametes

topics.neet_tip: Chromosome number calculations for the endosperm, zygote, egg and nucellus, and the products of syngamy versus triple fusion, are asked repeatedly.

topics.explanation: Endosperm development always precedes embryo development. The PEN usually undergoes free-nuclear divisions first and cellularisation later. In coconut, the water is free-nuclear endosperm with thousands of nuclei, and the white kernel is cellular endosperm. The endosperm may be fully consumed before seed maturity, as in pea, groundnut and beans, giving non-albuminous (exalbuminous) seeds. It may instead persist, as in wheat, maize, barley, castor and coconut, giving albuminous seeds. In a dicot, the embryo develops through proembryo, globular and heart-shaped stages to maturity. It has two cotyledons and an embryonal axis made of the epicotyl (ending in the plumule) and the hypocotyl (ending in the radicle and root cap). A monocot embryo has one cotyledon, the scutellum. Its radicle is enclosed in the coleorhiza and its plumule in the coleoptile. After fertilization the ovule becomes the seed, the integuments become the seed coats, and the ovary becomes the fruit, whose wall is the pericarp. In seeds the micropyle persists as a pore for entry of oxygen and water.
key_points: Persistent nucellus is called perisperm: black pepper, beet
Mature seeds have about 10-15% moisture and may enter dormancy
False fruits develop from the thalamus: apple, strawberry, cashew
True fruits develop from the ovary only
Lupinus arcticus seed germinated after about 10,000 years
Phoenix dactylifera (date palm) seed was about 2000 years old, recovered from King Herod's palace near the Dead Sea
Orchids produce tiny, numerous seeds; Orobanche and Striga are parasites with many tiny seeds
Monocot embryo parts: scutellum, coleoptile, coleorhiza

formulas.meaning: Ploidy of the parts of a seed

topics.neet_tip: Albuminous versus non-albuminous examples, perisperm, coconut endosperm and monocot embryo parts are standard one-liners.
topics.topic: Post-fertilization events: endosperm, embryo, seed and fruit

topics.explanation: Apomixis is the production of seeds without fertilization, so it is a form of asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction. It occurs in some Asteraceae and in grasses. In one route, a diploid egg cell forms without reduction division and develops into an embryo without fertilization. In another route, nucellus or integument cells divide and protrude into the embryo sac to form embryos. Polyembryony is the occurrence of more than one embryo in a seed, often from nucellar cells; examples are Citrus and mango. Apomixis is valuable because hybrid seed has to be bought fresh every year, since hybrid characters segregate in the next generation; apomictic hybrids would not segregate. Parthenocarpy is the formation of a fruit without fertilization, giving seedless fruits. Banana is the classic example, and parthenocarpy can be induced by applying growth hormones.
key_points: Apomixis gives seeds without fertilization, and the offspring are clones
Apomixis occurs in Asteraceae and grasses
Polyembryony: Citrus, mango (nucellar embryos)
Parthenocarpy gives fruits without fertilization: banana
Introducing apomictic genes into hybrids is a goal of crop scientists
topics.neet_tip: NEET contrasts apomixis (seed without fertilization) with parthenocarpy (fruit without fertilization) and asks for polyembryony examples.

topics.explanation: The male reproductive system lies in the pelvis. The testes are housed in the scrotum, which keeps them 2-2.5 degrees C below body temperature, as needed for spermatogenesis. Each testis is about 4-5 cm long and 2-3 cm wide and has about 250 testicular lobules, each with 1-3 seminiferous tubules. The duct pathway is seminiferous tubules, then rete testis, then vasa efferentia, then epididymis, then vas deferens, then ejaculatory duct, then urethra, which opens at the urethral meatus. The accessory glands are the paired seminal vesicles, the single prostate and the paired bulbourethral glands. Their secretions form seminal plasma, which is rich in fructose, calcium and enzymes; bulbourethral secretion helps lubricate the penis. The penis has an enlarged tip called the glans penis, covered by the foreskin. The female system has paired ovaries (2-4 cm), oviducts, uterus, cervix, vagina and external genitalia, together with the mammary glands. The oviduct is 10-12 cm long and has three parts: the infundibulum with its fimbriae, the ampulla and the isthmus. The uterine wall has three layers: the perimetrium, the myometrium and the endometrium.
key_points: Infundibulum, ampulla and isthmus are parts of the oviduct, not the male system
Male duct sequence: rete testis, vasa efferentia, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra
Myometrium shows strong contractions during parturition
Endometrium undergoes cyclical changes in the menstrual cycle
External female genitalia: mons pubis, labia majora, labia minora, hymen, clitoris
Mammary gland duct sequence: 15-20 mammary lobes with alveoli, then mammary tubules, mammary duct, mammary ampulla, lactiferous duct
topics.neet_tip: Questions ask whether a structure belongs to the male or female system, the correct duct sequence, and the layers of the uterus.

topics.explanation: In the testis, each seminiferous tubule is lined on its inside by two types of cells. Male germ cells (spermatogonia) undergo meiosis to form sperm. Sertoli cells nourish the germ cells. The interstitial spaces outside the tubules contain small blood vessels, immunocompetent cells and Leydig (interstitial) cells, which synthesise and secrete androgens such as testosterone. In the ovary, the stroma is divided into a peripheral cortex and an inner medulla. Follicles develop in stages. A primary follicle is a primary oocyte surrounded by granulosa cells. A secondary follicle has more granulosa layers and a new theca. A tertiary follicle has a fluid-filled antrum, and its theca is organised into theca interna and theca externa. The mature Graafian follicle holds a secondary oocyte surrounded by the zona pellucida. After ovulation, the follicle remnants form the corpus luteum.
key_points: Leydig cells secrete androgens; Sertoli cells nourish germ cells
Oocytes are surrounded by granulosa cells
The antrum first appears in the tertiary follicle
Zona pellucida is the covering around the secondary oocyte in the Graafian follicle and at ovulation
Many follicles degenerate by follicular atresia
topics.neet_tip: Identifying cell function (Leydig versus Sertoli) and follicle stages from diagram-based or statement-based questions is common.
topics.topic: Microscopic anatomy of testis and ovary

topics.explanation: Spermatogenesis begins at puberty. Spermatogonia ($2n = 46$) multiply by mitosis, and some become primary spermatocytes. Meiosis I gives two secondary spermatocytes ($n = 23$). Meiosis II gives four haploid spermatids. Spermatids transform into spermatozoa by spermiogenesis, and the sperm are released from the tubules by spermiation. The process is controlled by hormones: GnRH increases release of LH and FSH. LH acts on Leydig cells to stimulate androgens, and FSH acts on Sertoli cells to promote factors that aid spermiogenesis. A sperm has a head (nucleus and acrosome, which helps fertilization), a neck, a middle piece packed with mitochondria (energy for motility) and a tail. Oogenesis begins during foetal life. Oogonia form primary oocytes, which start meiosis but remain arrested in prophase I. No oogonia are added after birth. At puberty only 60,000-80,000 primary follicles remain in each ovary. The primary oocyte completes meiosis I in the tertiary follicle, giving a large haploid secondary oocyte and a tiny first polar body. Meiosis II is completed only when a sperm enters, giving the ovum and a second polar body.
key_points: Spermatogenesis starts at puberty; oogenesis starts in the foetus
Spermiogenesis converts spermatids into sperm; spermiation releases sperm
A normal ejaculate has 200-300 million sperm
For normal fertility, at least 60% of sperm should have normal shape and at least 40% should show vigorous motility
Primary oocyte remains arrested in prophase I until puberty
Unequal cytokinesis in oogenesis produces polar bodies
The secondary oocyte completes meiosis II only after sperm entry

formulas.meaning: Calculating sperm number from spermatocyte number
Calculating ova number; only one functional gamete forms

formulas.formula: $\text{Spermatogonia, primary spermatocyte} = 2n; \; \text{secondary spermatocyte, spermatid, sperm} = n$

topics.neet_tip: NEET tests the ploidy of each stage, the targets of LH and FSH in the male, and the stage at which oocyte meiosis is arrested and completed.

topics.explanation: The menstrual cycle is the reproductive cycle of female primates. It averages about 28/29 days, begins at menarche at puberty and stops at menopause, around 50 years. The menstrual phase lasts 3-5 days, when the endometrium breaks down because the ovum was not fertilized. In the follicular (proliferative) phase, rising FSH and LH drive follicle growth, and the follicle secretes estrogen, which regenerates the endometrium. LH and FSH peak around mid-cycle, about day 14, and this LH surge induces rupture of the Graafian follicle, which is ovulation. In the luteal (secretory) phase, the corpus luteum secretes large amounts of progesterone, which maintains the endometrium for implantation. If no fertilization occurs, the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls and menstruation follows. Pregnancy stops the cycle.
key_points: Phases: menstrual, follicular (proliferative), ovulatory, luteal (secretory)
LH surge causes ovulation around day 14
Corpus luteum secretes mainly progesterone, which maintains the endometrium
Estrogen peaks before ovulation
Lack of menstruation may indicate pregnancy, stress or poor health

formulas.meaning: Luteal phase is roughly constant at 14 days

topics.neet_tip: Statement-type questions check that the LH surge causes ovulation and that the corpus luteum secretes progesterone, not mainly estrogen.

topics.explanation: Fertilisation occurs at the ampullary-isthmic junction of the oviduct. When a sperm contacts the zona pellucida, changes in the membrane block entry of additional sperm. Acrosomal enzymes help the sperm enter the cytoplasm of the secondary oocyte, which then completes meiosis II, giving the ovum and a second polar body. The haploid nuclei fuse to form a diploid zygote. Sex is decided by the sperm: an X sperm gives a female (XX) and a Y sperm gives a male (XY). The zygote undergoes mitotic cleavage as it moves toward the uterus, forming blastomeres. The 8-16 cell embryo is the morula. The morula becomes a blastocyst with an outer trophoblast and an inner cell mass. The trophoblast attaches to the endometrium, the uterine cells cover the blastocyst, and the blastocyst becomes embedded. This embedding is implantation, and it leads to pregnancy.
key_points: Site of fertilisation: ampullary-isthmic junction
Only one sperm fertilises an ovum because of the block to polyspermy
Morula: 8-16 blastomeres
Blastocyst: trophoblast (outer) plus inner cell mass
Inner cell mass contains stem cells that give rise to all tissues and organs
Implantation occurs in the endometrium of the uterus
topics.neet_tip: NEET asks the site of fertilisation, the morula cell count, the fate of the trophoblast versus the inner cell mass, and the role of the father in sex determination.
topics.topic: Fertilisation, embryo development up to blastocyst and implantation

topics.explanation: After implantation, finger-like chorionic villi grow from the trophoblast and interdigitate with uterine tissue to form the placenta. The placenta supplies oxygen and nutrients to the embryo, removes carbon dioxide and wastes, and is connected to the embryo by the umbilical cord. It acts as an endocrine tissue, secreting hCG, hPL, estrogens and progestogens. Relaxin is secreted by the ovary in later pregnancy. Placental hormones together with raised maternal hormones support pregnancy. The inner cell mass differentiates into ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. Human gestation lasts about 9 months. Parturition starts with the foetal ejection reflex, which comes from the fully developed foetus and placenta. This triggers oxytocin release, causing stronger uterine contractions in a positive feedback loop. Lactation begins toward the end of pregnancy. The first milk, colostrum, contains IgA antibodies that give passive immunity to the newborn.
key_points: Hormones of pregnancy only: hCG, hPL, relaxin
LH and FSH are not placental hormones
Development timeline: heart forms after 1 month; limbs and digits by the end of month 2
By the end of 12 weeks (first trimester), most organ systems, limbs and external genitalia have formed
First foetal movements and hair on the head appear in the 5th month
By the end of 24 weeks, the body has fine hair, the eyelids separate and eyelashes form
Oxytocin acts on the uterine myometrium during parturition
Colostrum is rich in IgA antibodies
topics.neet_tip: Common questions: which hormone is not placental (LH, FSH), the foetal development timeline, and the role of oxytocin and colostrum.
topics.topic: Pregnancy, placenta formation, parturition and lactation

topics.explanation: The WHO describes reproductive health as total well-being in the physical, emotional, behavioural and social aspects of reproduction. India was among the first countries to start a national family planning programme, in 1951. These efforts were later expanded as Reproductive and Child Health Care (RCH) programmes. Sexually transmitted infections (STIs), also called venereal or reproductive tract infections, include gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, chlamydiasis, genital warts, trichomoniasis, hepatitis B and HIV/AIDS. Hepatitis B and HIV are also spread by sharing needles, transfusion of infected blood and from mother to foetus. Except for hepatitis B, genital herpes and HIV, the others are completely curable if detected early. They are most common in the 15-24 years age group. Untreated STIs can lead to pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), abortions, still births, ectopic pregnancy, infertility and cancer of the reproductive tract. Prevention includes avoiding sex with unknown or multiple partners, always using condoms, and seeking early medical help.
key_points: Tuberculosis, typhoid and cholera are not STIs
Not completely curable: hepatitis B, genital herpes, HIV
Highest STI incidence is in persons aged 15-24 years
Population was about 350 million in 1947, about 1 billion in 2000 and about 1.2 billion in 2011
Statutory marriageable age is 18 years for females and 21 years for males
Reduced MMR and IMR, and increased life expectancy, contributed to population growth
topics.neet_tip: NEET frequently asks which disease is not an STD, or which STDs are incurable.
topics.topic: Reproductive health and prevention of STDs

topics.explanation: An ideal contraceptive is user-friendly, easily available, effective, reversible and has no or few side effects. Natural methods include periodic abstinence (avoiding coitus on days 10-17 of the cycle), withdrawal (coitus interruptus) and lactational amenorrhea, which is effective for up to 6 months after parturition. Barrier methods are condoms (Nirodh for males, and female condoms), diaphragms, cervical caps and vaults, often used with spermicidal creams. IUDs are of three kinds: non-medicated (Lippes loop), copper-releasing (CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375), which suppress sperm motility, and hormone-releasing (Progestasert, LNG-20), which make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperm. Oral pills contain progestogens or progestogen-estrogen combinations, taken for 21 days starting within the first five days of the cycle. They inhibit ovulation and implantation. Saheli, a once-a-week pill, was developed at CDRI Lucknow. Emergency contraception (pills, IUD) is effective within 72 hours of coitus. Surgical sterilisation is vasectomy in males and tubectomy in females. MTP is safe in the first trimester. Under the MTP (Amendment) Act 2017, termination within 12 weeks needs the opinion of one registered medical practitioner, and termination between 12 and 24 weeks needs two.
key_points: Copper IUDs suppress sperm motility and fertilising capacity
Hormonal IUDs make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperm
Saheli is a non-steroidal, once-a-week pill from CDRI Lucknow
Vasectomy removes or ties a small part of the vas deferens; tubectomy does the same to the fallopian tube
Surgical methods have very poor reversibility
About 45-50 million MTPs occur worldwide each year, about one-fifth of all pregnancies
IUDs are ideal for females who want to delay pregnancy or space children
topics.neet_tip: Matching contraceptives to their type or mode of action, Saheli facts, the emergency window and MTP time limits are very frequently tested.
topics.topic: Birth control: methods, contraception and MTP

topics.explanation: Amniocentesis is a prenatal diagnostic technique. A small sample of amniotic fluid surrounding the developing foetus is withdrawn, and the foetal cells and dissolved substances in it are analysed. It detects chromosomal abnormalities such as Down syndrome and some genetic or metabolic disorders. Because the karyotype also reveals the sex of the foetus, it has been misused for sex determination, which led to female foeticide. Its use for sex determination is therefore legally banned in India. Its legitimate use is to identify serious foetal disorders, so that informed decisions, including MTP under the legal framework, can be made.
key_points: Analyses foetal cells in amniotic fluid
Detects chromosomal and genetic abnormalities
Use for sex determination is legally banned in India
Misuse is linked to female foeticide
topics.neet_tip: NEET asks what amniocentesis detects and why its misuse for sex determination is banned.

topics.explanation: Infertility is the inability to conceive despite unprotected cohabitation. It may arise from physical, congenital, immunological, psychological or drug-related causes, in either the male or the female partner. Assisted reproductive technologies (ART) help such couples. In IVF-ET (in vitro fertilisation followed by embryo transfer, the test tube baby method), gametes are fused outside the body and the embryo is transferred into the woman. In ZIFT, a zygote or early embryo with up to 8 blastomeres is transferred into the fallopian tube. In IUT, an embryo with more than 8 blastomeres is transferred into the uterus. Embryos formed by in vivo fertilisation can also be transferred. In GIFT, an ovum collected from a donor is transferred into the fallopian tube of a female who cannot produce ova but can provide a suitable environment for fertilisation and development. In ICSI, a sperm is injected directly into the ovum. Artificial insemination (AI), including intra-uterine insemination (IUI), is used when the male has a low sperm count or cannot inseminate.
key_points: ZIFT: embryo with up to 8 blastomeres placed in the fallopian tube
IUT: embryo with more than 8 blastomeres placed in the uterus
GIFT: ovum, not zygote, is transferred into the fallopian tube
ICSI: sperm injected directly into the ovum
AI or IUI: semen from the husband or a donor introduced into the vagina or uterus
ART is costly and needs specialised professionals; emotional, religious and social factors limit its use, and legal adoption is an alternative

formulas.meaning: Deciding the transfer site from the embryo stage

topics.neet_tip: NEET asks which technique matches which description, such as ICSI for direct sperm injection, GIFT for ovum transfer, and ZIFT versus IUT by blastomere count.
topics.topic: Infertility and assisted reproductive technologies: IVF, ZIFT, GIFT

common_traps: Thinking the corpus luteum mainly secretes estrogen; it secretes large amounts of progesterone.
Thinking geitonogamy is genetic cross-pollination; it is genetically similar to autogamy because the pollen comes from the same plant.
Assuming every aquatic plant is water-pollinated; water hyacinth and water lily are pollinated by insects or wind.
Thinking monoecious plants such as maize and castor prevent geitonogamy; they prevent only autogamy, while dioecious papaya prevents both.
Confusing GIFT with ZIFT; GIFT transfers an ovum, while ZIFT transfers a zygote or early embryo with up to 8 blastomeres.
Listing LH or FSH as placental hormones; the placenta secretes hCG, hPL, estrogens and progestogens.
Believing meiosis in the oocyte is completed before ovulation; meiosis II is completed only after sperm entry.
Taking the endosperm as diploid; it is triploid, formed from one male gamete plus two polar nuclei.
quick_revision: Anther: 2 lobes x 2 thecae = 4 microsporangia; the innermost wall layer, the tapetum, is nutritive
Embryo sac: 1 meiosis plus 3 mitoses gives 8 nuclei in 7 cells; synergids with filiform apparatus guide the pollen tube
Double fertilization: syngamy gives the $2n$ zygote and triple fusion gives the $3n$ PEN
Cleistogamy: Viola, Oxalis, Commelina; water pollination: Vallisneria, Zostera; Yucca is pollinated by a moth
Albuminous: cereals, castor, coconut; non-albuminous: pea, groundnut, beans; perisperm: black pepper, beet
Apomixis gives seed without fertilization; parthenocarpy gives fruit without fertilization (banana); polyembryony: Citrus, mango
Male duct path: rete testis, vasa efferentia, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra
Oogenesis starts in the foetus and arrests at prophase I; the secondary oocyte at ovulation is covered by the zona pellucida
Cycle: menstrual (3-5 days), follicular (estrogen), LH surge and ovulation (about day 14), luteal (progesterone)
Fertilisation at the ampullary-isthmic junction; morula is 8-16 cells; blastocyst has trophoblast plus inner cell mass
Parturition: foetal ejection reflex leads to oxytocin release; colostrum carries IgA
ART: ICSI injects sperm into the ovum; GIFT transfers an ovum; ZIFT for up to 8 blastomeres; IUT for more than 8 blastomeres
